sections.html:
A Sayreville seller needs a Certificate of Residential Resale Compliance from the borough and, separately, a smoke, carbon monoxide and secondary power source certificate from the Bureau of Fire Prevention. The fire marshal's 2026 sheet makes the second one a requirement for closing whatever the condition of the house and whatever the contract says about as-is terms.

Sayreville sits on the south bank of the Raritan River in Middlesex County, with an estimated 46,787 residents in July 2025 across 17,187 households. Median home value is $444,100, 63.0 percent of households own, and 33.3 percent of residents were born outside the United States, so listing material in more than one language reaches more buyers.

sections.h2: How to book the resale inspection
sections.html:
The borough takes resale applications online. Create an account, fill in the application and submit it. The office emails the fee, usually within one business day. After you pay online, request an appointment. Resale inspections run on Mondays and Wednesdays, and rental inspections on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

Call as soon as the house is listed so the office can check the file for open permits. The inspector looks hard at recently installed water heaters, furnaces and finished basements, and a permit that was never closed out can hold up the certificate.

Offices to call during a Sayreville sale
OfficePhoneWhat it handles
Code Enforcement732-390-7077Resale compliance application
Bureau of Fire Prevention, 167 Main Street732-390-7009Alarm inspection
Water Department732-390-7060Curb stop and final reading
Middlesex County Board of Taxation732-745-3350Assessment appeals

Violations bring a correction notice and a reinspection before the certificate is released. Inspectors may also cite other violations of the International Property Maintenance Code and borough ordinances.

  • Exit doors must open from inside without a key, and double-keyed deadbolts are prohibited.
  • Stairs with three or more steps need a handrail, and house numbers must be at least 4 inches tall and visible from the street.
  • Kitchen stoves need anti-tip devices, and a single-family house may have only one working kitchen.
  • A basement, attic or garage used as a bedroom must meet habitable-space rules, including an approved egress window that needs a construction permit, or the house fails.
  • Pools deeper than 18 inches need a fence at least 48 inches high with a self-closing, self-latching gate.
  • The water curb stop must work, so call the Water Department before closing.

A house sold as-is is still subject to permit requirements. Any missing permit has to be applied for and finalized by a contractor, which is worth settling before an offer comes in.

Alarms are required on every finished level, within 10 feet of each sleeping area, at the bottom of basement stairs, and in finished attics with 7 feet or more of ceiling height. Smoke alarms must be under 10 years old, and stand-alone battery units must be 10-year sealed. Carbon monoxide alarms must be under 7 years old. Devices that belong to a home security system do not count, so stand-alone units go beside them.

Since February 3, 2025, a house with solar panels, battery storage or a generator must display a printed label reading "CAUTION: MULTIPLE SOURCES OF POWER," fixed within 18 inches of the main panel and the meter. Handwritten labels are rejected. Portable fire extinguishers are no longer part of resale inspections, and the fire marshal asks owners to drop old ones at a Middlesex County household hazardous waste day.

sections.h2: If the house fails the first visit
sections.html:
A failed visit is common and it is not the end of the sale. The borough sends a correction notice listing each violation. Fix the items, then ask the office for a reinspection before the certificate is released. Nothing is released until the list is cleared.

Finished basements, converted garages and attic bedrooms cause the most trouble. If a room was made into a bedroom without a permit, it must meet habitable-space rules, and that includes an approved egress window, which itself needs a construction permit. If the cost of bringing a room up to standard is more than you want to spend, say so to your attorney early, because the buyer will want to know before the contract is final.

Smaller failures tend to be cheap: a detector past its age limit, a missing handrail on stairs with three or more steps, an anti-tip device missing from the stove, or a house number too small to read from the street. Fix those before the first visit and the inspection becomes a formality.

Low-lying ground near the river floods in storm surges. After Hurricane Sandy in 2012, residents accepted a federally funded offer in 2013 to buy out 250 floodplain houses. If your house is near the water, gather any flood insurance and elevation records before listing, since buyers and their lenders will ask for them.

The borough uses four ZIP codes, 08871, 08872, 08879 and 08859. Use the one on your deed and tax record when you list and when you fill in the resale application, so the file matches. A mismatch between the application, the deed and the listing is a small thing that can cost a day or two at the counter.

sections.h2: Costs and tax steps at closing
sections.html:
The Middlesex County Board of Taxation is at 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, New Brunswick, and takes petitions through an online portal. Its added or omitted assessment deadline is December 1. Ask the board for the regular filing date for Sayreville.

The seller owes the state transfer fee, with each band of the schedule applying to the slice of price inside it. A corporation, partnership or multi-member LLC signs a GIT/REP-3 and checks box 5. An individual seller who lives out of state pays at least 2 percent of the deed price in estimated tax unless an assurance applies.

sections.h2: A timeline for a quick Sayreville sale
sections.html:
Work backward from the closing date and give each office room to answer.

  1. As soon as the house is listed, call Code Enforcement so the permit file gets checked.
  2. Create the online account, submit the application and pay the emailed fee.
  3. Choose a Monday or Wednesday for the resale visit and run through the checklist the evening before.
  4. Arrange the alarm inspection with the Bureau of Fire Prevention.
  5. Fix anything on the correction notice and ask for the reinspection.
  6. Give both certificates to the closing attorney.

A cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands avoids repair haggling, but both certificates are still required for closing, so budget time for them whichever route you choose.

faqs.q: What is the Sayreville Certificate of Residential Resale Compliance?
faqs.a: It is the borough's clearance after an inspection against a 20-item checklist covering life safety, interior conditions, building systems, exterior conditions and permits. It is separate from the fire marshal's alarm certificate.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Sayreville house as-is without these inspections?
faqs.a: No. The alarm certificate is required for closing despite any as-is terms, and as-is houses are not exempt from permit requirements.

faqs.q: On which days are Sayreville resale inspections held?
faqs.a: Mondays and Wednesdays. Rental inspections are on Tuesdays and Thursdays. You request a date after paying the emailed fee online.

faqs.q: Do I need a fire extinguisher for the Sayreville inspection?
faqs.a: No. Since February 3, 2025, state law no longer requires one for resale inspections. Solar, battery or generator systems need a printed power-source warning label instead.
